title: After amrit
hook: a new beginning, not the end of learning
tomorrow: Simran's decided: not yet. so is she less of a Sikh?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a closed door, an iron bowl, and sugar stirred with steel: the five give. Jasleen came out grinning. Two mornings later, she isn't.

An alarm set for early. Snoozed once, then twice, then the sun is up and the quiet hour is gone. Jasleen texts Simran a single word: ruined. She took amrit on Sunday. On Tuesday she slept straight through her morning Nitnem for the first time. Now she's sure she's broken it already, two days in, and maybe she was never ready at all. Simran stares at the word on her screen. She has no idea what to send back.
screen: `SNOOZE. SNOOZE. SUNRISE.` → `ONE WORD: RUINED.` → `WHAT DO YOU SEND BACK?`

segments.voice: Here's what the Sikh code of conduct says right after the ceremony, and it's the answer for Jasleen. The newly initiated are told who their family is now. Their father is Guru Gobind Singh. Their mother is Mata Sahib Kaur. Their home is Anandpur Sahib. That's the language of a birth, not a graduation. Amrit isn't a diploma for someone who's done learning. It's being born into a family where the learning starts, and newborns don't get everything right in their first week. The code expects stumbles, too. When an amritdhari Sikh breaks the rehat, there's a way back: go before five Sikhs, say it plainly, and accept a tankhah, a penance such as extra prayer or seva. The door back in is built into the path. And the Granth is honest about all of us. On ang 61, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: everyone makes mistakes; only the Guru and the Creator never err. A missed morning isn't one of the four things avoided. It's a missed morning. The rhythm is still the goal, and tomorrow's dawn still comes. So Simran types: you're two days old. babies sleep in. get up tomorrow and start again. Jasleen sends back a laughing face, and then: ok. tomorrow.
screen: `A NEW FAMILY, A NEW HOME.` · `A BIRTH, NOT A GRADUATION.` · `TANKHAH: A WAY BACK IN.` · `ANG 61: EVERYONE MAKES MISTAKES.` · then, large: `A NEW BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you meant to start and let slide: a habit, a call, a page of reading. Do the smallest possible piece of it now, even just one line or one stretch. Then sit, and let it count as day one again.
After amrit. A birth into the Khalsa family, where the learning begins rather than ends.
Keep this one: a new beginning, and missed mornings come with a way back in. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1657 COUNTS.` → `LIVING IT · 31 OF 134.` → `TOMORROW: SIMRAN'S NOT YET. IS SHE LESS OF A SIKH?`

howItsDone: After the ceremony the five explain the rehat and name the Khalsa's spiritual father, mother and home. An amritdhari Sikh who breaks the rehat can go before five Sikhs and accept a tankhah, a penance.

chat.says: jasleen overslept her nitnem on DAY 2 and thinks she ruined everything. what do i say
options: amrit's a birth, not a finish line. one missed morning isn't ruin; start again tomorrow.
she's right; one missed morning means she'll need the ceremony all over again.
tell her to skip it for a while; nitnem is optional once you've taken amrit.
chat.meaning: The code speaks of amrit as a birth into a new family, with a way back built in. Everyone makes mistakes, says ang 61.

Mata Sahib Kaur.meaning: named in the code as the Khalsa's mother

Anandpur Sahib.meaning: a town in Punjab, named as the Khalsa's home

tankhah.meaning: a penance accepted after breaking the rehat

sources.ref: Sikh Rehat Maryada, section on the amrit ceremony (the spiritual father, mother and home named) and on tankhah (penance for breaches), paraphrased
Ang 61 (Sri Raag, Guru Nanak: bhulan andar sabh ko abhul guru kartar), paraphrased

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape life (a missed morning two days after amrit; what the tradition gives you for it). Storyline: Jasleen texts 'ruined'; Simran answers. Pacing: Simran still hasn't decided for herself.
Confirm the ang for 'bhulan andar sabh ko abhul guru kartar' (Sri Raag, Guru Nanak; given as ang 61).

'A missed morning isn't one of the four things avoided' is meant to distinguish a lapse in Nitnem from a kurahit; the code treats skipping Nitnem as a matter for tankhah in some readings. A Keeper may want the wording adjusted ('pick it up again, and ask the sangat if unsure').
Tankhah examples ('extra prayer or seva') are summarized; confirm.
